834.title: The crow in Babylon
834.hook: a crow is prized in a foreign land until a peacock arrives (Jataka 339)
834.howItsDone: The Pali texts name eight worldly conditions that keep the world turning: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. Teachers use tales like this one to show praise leaving as easily as it came.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hare, the falling fruit on the palm leaf, and the lion who went back to check. Your line was check first. Did a rumor stop with you? Today, a new week, and a long voyage by sea. Day eight hundred thirty-four.

In the land of Baveru, the tale says, there were no birds at all. Some readers take Baveru to be Babylon. Into this birdless country sail merchants from far away, and they've brought a crow along on the ship. An ordinary black crow. The people of Baveru crowd the dock to see it. They have never seen anything like it, and they can't stop talking about it. Today, the crow in Babylon.
screen: `A LAND WITH NO BIRDS.` → `MERCHANTS ARRIVE BY SHIP.` → `AN ORDINARY BLACK CROW.`

segments.voice: First, the crow's glory. The people of Baveru praise everything about it: the gloss of its feathers, its beak, its voice. They buy it for a high price, keep it in a fine cage, and feed it meat and fruit. For a while, a plain crow is the talk of the country. Second, the peacock. On a later voyage, the merchants bring a peacock, trained to cry out at a snap of the fingers and to dance at a clap of the hands. The people are dazzled. It sells for far more than the crow ever did. Third, the crow forgotten. From that day nobody brings the crow its meat and fruit. It flies off, and the tale leaves it scratching for scraps in a rubbish heap. The tale's verse says it plainly: until the peacock came, they honored the crow. Fourth, reading it. The crow did nothing wrong. It never changed. It was a crow when they praised it, and a crow when they forgot it. It was prized because nothing else was there, and dropped the moment something brighter arrived. So the praise was never quite about the crow. Praise that depends on there being no peacock was always borrowed. And the crow was a perfectly good crow before Baveru, and after. Being ordinary was never the loss; the praise was only ever a season.
screen: `THE CROW IN A FINE CAGE.` · `A PEACOCK THAT DANCES.` · `NOBODY FEEDS THE CROW.` · `IT NEVER CHANGED.` · then, large: `THEN THE PEACOCK CAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit as an ordinary person on an ordinary day. No achievement to admire, no audience. Feel the plain things: your weight on the seat, the air at your nose, a sound somewhere in the room. None of it is special. See whether that's restful. Let the peacocks dance somewhere else. Later today, enjoy one ordinary thing about yourself without needing anyone to notice it. The bell holds the time.
Mayura. Peacock: the bird whose arrival ended a plain crow's glory in a land with no birds, in a Jataka tale. Today's word.
Your line: then the peacock came. Today, when praise comes or goes, remember the crow, and enjoy being ordinary. Day eight hundred thirty-four.

fork.setup: you're the crow. the peacock has arrived, and nobody brings you food anymore. what happens?
options: you learn to dance.
you fly off and find your own scraps.
you pick a fight with the peacock.
fork.reveal: the crow, forgotten, flies off to a rubbish heap. it was a crow all along; only the praise had changed.

original.note: Pali: mayura, peacock, the bird whose arrival ends the crow's glory.

trapdoor: what you thought: a funny story about a vain crow.
what it means: praise that depends on there being no rival was never really about the crow.
what a scholar hears: the tale is the Baveru Jataka; its merchants sail to Baveru, which some readers identify with Babylon.

835.title: The jackal's judgment
835.hook: two otters quarrel over a fish; the jackal judge takes the middle (Jataka 400)
835.howItsDone: The monastic code, the Vinaya, sets out ways for monks and nuns to settle disputes within the community themselves, and this tale's frame is about a dispute settled badly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crow in Babylon, prized until the mayura, the peacock, arrived. Your line was then the peacock came. Did you enjoy being ordinary? Today, two otters and one very large fish. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

On a riverbank, two otters are hunting together, one working the deep water, one along the shore. The deep-water otter bites into a huge fish, and the fish is so strong it starts dragging him under. He calls out, and his partner rushes in. Between them they wrestle it up onto the bank, and lie there panting, very pleased. Then one of them says: so, how do we split it? Today, the jackal's judgment.
screen: `TWO OTTERS HUNTING.` → `A FISH TOO BIG FOR ONE.` → `HOW DO WE SPLIT IT?`

segments.voice: First, the teamwork. Neither otter could have landed that fish alone. It took both of them, one in the deep and one on the shore. Second, the quarrel. Now that the fish is on the bank, each is sure he deserves the better share. One caught it; the other saved him. Neither will give an inch, and the argument goes round and round. Third, the judge. A jackal comes down to the river to drink, and the otters, tired of arguing, ask him to settle it. The jackal is happy to oblige. He gives the tail to the otter who worked the shore, and the head to the otter who went into the deep. And the whole middle, the meat of the fish, he takes for himself as his fee for judging. Off he trots. The otters are left on the bank, staring at a head and a tail. Fourth, the point. Back home, the jackal's wife asks how a jackal who can't fish came by a fish like that, and his answer in the verse is blunt: quarrels make people thin, and the otters' quarrel fed him. The frame of the tale tells of a greedy monk who settled a dispute between two others over some robes, and kept the best one for himself. The jackal didn't have to fight anyone or steal anything. The quarrel did the work for him. If the otters had split the fish themselves, even unevenly, each would have eaten well. A fair settlement made by the people involved keeps the fish whole.
screen: `TWO OTTERS LAND A FISH.` · `WHO GETS THE BETTER SHARE?` · `THE JACKAL JUDGES.` · `HEAD, TAIL, AND NO MIDDLE.` · then, large: `THE JUDGE ATE THE FISH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring to mind a small quarrel that's still open. Over chores, money, who said what. Sit with both sides of it, as the fair judge would, not the jackal. What's really yours? What's really theirs? What's the middle that's being lost while the argument goes on? Breathe with it. Later today, settle one quarrel fairly, even a small one, before it needs a jackal. The bell holds the time.
Quarrel. What fed the jackal, called in to judge between two otters fighting over their catch, who walked off with the middle himself. Today's word.
Your line: the judge ate the fish. Today, settle one quarrel fairly while there's still a fish to share. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fable about a sly jackal.
what it means: when we can't settle a quarrel ourselves, the one who settles it may take the best part.
what a scholar hears: the tale's frame tells of a greedy monk who settled a dispute over robes and kept the best one himself.

836.title: Two chariots
836.hook: two gods meet on a narrow road; the unrighteous won't yield and falls (Jataka 457)
836.howItsDone: Dhamma, the Pali form of the Sanskrit dharma, is one of the Three Jewels Buddhists take refuge in, together with the Buddha and the Sangha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two otters' quarrel, one fish, and the jackal who judged between them. Your line was the judge ate the fish. Did you settle something fairly? Today, a narrow road, high in the air. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

Two chariots, nose to nose on a road with room for only one, and neither driver will back up. It could be any narrow lane on any weekday morning. In this Jataka tale the road runs through the sky, and the drivers are gods. One is named Dhamma, righteousness. The other is Adhamma, its opposite. Each has somewhere to be, and each expects the other to move. Today, two chariots.
screen: `A ROAD WITH ROOM FOR ONE.` → `TWO GODS, NOSE TO NOSE.` → `DHAMMA AND ADHAMMA.`

segments.voice: First, the meeting. In the tale, both gods travel through the world in their chariots, and one day their paths cross head on, in a place where only one can pass. Second, the claims. Each tells the other to get out of the way, and each makes his case. Adhamma's case is force: he is strong, and he does not give way to anyone. Dhamma's case is his goodness, and the honor the wise give it. Third, the refusal. Adhamma will not yield. Not an inch. He even offers to fight for the road. Dhamma's answer, in the tale's last verse between them, is that if Adhamma really is the stronger, he'll swallow the harsh words and make way for him. And at the very moment Dhamma says it, Adhamma topples from his chariot headfirst, and the earth opens and swallows him. Fourth, the road goes on. Dhamma, the Bodhisatta in this tale, continues on his way. The story doesn't have Dhamma win by shoving harder. He never rams the other chariot. The one who insists on never yielding is the one who falls, and the road opens for the one who was willing to give it up. Some readers find the whole point in that fall: what cannot bend at all eventually breaks. On an ordinary road, letting someone go first costs a few seconds. In a family argument it might cost a little pride. The tale suggests that refusing can cost a great deal more. So yielding here isn't weakness, and it isn't losing. It's how the road stays open.
screen: `TWO GODS, ONE NARROW ROAD.` · `EACH CLAIMS THE WAY.` · `ADHAMMA WILL NOT YIELD.` · `THE STUBBORN ONE FALLS.` · then, large: `YIELDING WINS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit, and find somewhere in the body that's braced. Shoulders, jaw, hands. That's the body refusing to give way. Breathe out, and let it yield a little. Then think of one place today where you'll meet someone head on: a doorway, a meeting, a merge on the road, a conversation that tends to dig in. Decide now to let them go first, once. The bell holds the time.
Two chariots. A Jataka tale: righteousness and its opposite meet on a narrow road, and the one who will not yield is the one who falls. Today's word.
Your line: yielding wins. Today, yield once, on purpose, and notice what it actually costs. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

original.note: Pali: dhamma, the teaching, what is right; in this tale it is also the name of the righteous god.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about road rage among gods.
what it means: the one who will not yield is the one who falls, and the road stays open for the other.
what a scholar hears: the names are a pair, dhamma and adhamma, righteousness and its negation, and in the tale Dhamma is the Bodhisatta.

837.title: King Sivi's eyes
837.hook: a king gives his eyes to a blind beggar (Jataka 499)
837.howItsDone: The Sivi story is told in Buddhist teaching as an example of the perfection of giving (dana); everyday generosity takes smaller forms, like food offered to monastics, gifts to people in need, or time given freely.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two chariots met on a narrow road, and the one who would not give way was the one who fell. Your line was yielding wins. Did you let someone pass first? Today, a king who gives up far more than the road. Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

Some gifts cost nothing. Spare change, an old coat, a favor that fits the afternoon. King Sivi, in the Jataka, had given plenty of those: food, clothes, money, the story says, and he still wanted to give more. One day he made a quiet wish. If anyone ever asked for a part of his own body, he would give it. Then someone asked. A blind old man came before the king and asked for an eye. Here is what Sivi did next.
screen: `GIFTS THAT COST NOTHING.` → `A KING'S QUIET WISH.` → `A BLIND MAN ASKS FOR AN EYE.`

segments.voice: First, the test. The blind man wasn't what he seemed. The Jataka says he was Sakka, king of the gods, in disguise, come to see whether Sivi meant his wish. Second, the cost. The king's ministers pleaded with him. Give gold, they said, give jewels, give anything, but not your eyes. Sivi sent for his surgeon anyway. The story doesn't hurry here. It dwells on the pain, and it has the king say he isn't giving for gain; he gives for the sake of awakening. And once the first eye was given, he gave the second. Third, the aftermath. Blind now, Sivi left the palace and sat alone by a pond. Sakka came back and asked him to speak the truth about his gift. The king said, truthfully, that he had given gladly. On those true words, the story says, his sight returned. Fourth, how to hold a story this extreme. It isn't a recipe for harming yourself. Tradition tells it as a picture of the perfection of giving, dana, stretched as far as it can go. Its question for an ordinary Tuesday is smaller and sharper: is there a gift that would actually cost you something? Not money, necessarily. An hour you'd guarded. Credit you'd love to keep. An apology that bruises your pride. Sivi's tale isn't about the size of a gift. It's about giving past the part of you that would rather hold back.
screen: `A BEGGAR WHO WASN'T A BEGGAR.` · `GIVE GOLD, NOT YOUR EYES.` · `TRUE WORDS, AND SIGHT RETURNS.` · `A GIFT THAT COSTS YOU.` · then, large: `WHAT HE GAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the gift that costs. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle on its own. Then ask, quietly, what you could give today that you'd rather keep. Time. Attention. A word of credit. Patience with someone who wears yours thin. Let a few answers come and go. Don't pick the biggest. Pick the one that's real, one you can actually give before tonight. Then, for the rest of the sit, notice the part of you that wants to hold on. You don't have to argue with it. Just see it there. The bell holds the time.
Dana. Giving: the perfection King Sivi showed, a gift given whole, what he would most want to keep, asked for nothing back. Today's word.
Your line: what he gave. Give the one costly thing you chose, and don't mention what it cost you. Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: a grim old legend about a king and his eyes.

what a scholar hears: in Jataka 499 the gift ends with an act of truth, true words that restore his sight, the same device as the fish king who brought the rain.

838.title: The six-tusked elephant
838.hook: an elephant helps the hunter who wounded him cut his tusks (Jataka 514)
838.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers retell the Chaddanta story as a tale of patience and forgiveness; Buddhists practice letting go of resentment through reflection and loving-kindness meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Sivi's dana, his giving, gave both his eyes to a blind stranger. Your line was what he gave. Did you give the thing that cost you? Today, a gift given to an enemy. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

The arrow comes from below. An elephant king walks a forest path, and a hunter hidden in a pit shoots a poisoned arrow up into him. In the Jataka this elephant is Chaddanta, the six-tusked, the leader of a great herd. The story could end with him crushing the man in the pit. Every part of him has the strength to do it. It doesn't end that way. Today, what the wounded elephant does instead.
screen: `AN ARROW FROM BELOW.` → `A HUNTER IN A PIT.` → `THE STRENGTH TO CRUSH HIM.`

segments.voice: First, how it started. Chaddanta had two wives, and one of them, Culla-subhadda, came to believe he favored the other. The slight was small, the story makes clear: a shower of blossoms that fell on the wrong wife. She nursed it until she died wishing for revenge, and she was reborn as a queen in a human kingdom. Second, the hunter. As queen, she sent a hunter named Sonuttara to find the elephant and bring back his tusks. He made the long journey and hid in a pit, wearing the yellow robe of a renunciant. Third, the turn. Wounded, Chaddanta went for him, then saw the robe and stopped. He would not harm someone wearing that cloth, even someone wearing it as a trick. He asked the hunter why, and heard about the queen, and understood who wanted him dead. Then the hunter tried to saw off the tusks and couldn't manage it. So Chaddanta took the saw in his own trunk, cut the tusks himself, handed them over, and died. Fourth, what the tale doesn't say. It doesn't say the wound didn't matter. It doesn't call the hunter good. It shows someone who had every right to strike back, and chose to help instead. When the queen saw the tusks, the story says, she remembered who he had been, and grief overwhelmed her. The grudge ran the whole story. The elephant is the one who stopped it.
screen: `A GRUDGE OVER FALLING BLOSSOMS.` · `A HUNTER IN A YELLOW ROBE.` · `HE STOPS, AND ASKS WHY.` · `THE SAW IN HIS OWN TRUNK.` · then, large: `HE HELPED THE HUNTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: loosen one hurt. Sit and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind a small injury, not the biggest one you carry. A sharp word. A slight at work. Someone who took the credit. See if you can find where it sits in the body, the jaw, the chest, the stomach. You don't have to excuse it or call it fine. Just try, for one breath, setting it down, the way the elephant stopped at the sight of a robe. If it comes back, notice that too, and set it down again. The bell holds the time.
Chaddanta. The six-tusked elephant king who, wounded by a hunter, helped him take the tusks he came for. Today's word.
Your line: he helped the hunter. When the small hurt you chose comes back today, answer it with one helpful act instead of a sharp one. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

original.note: Pali Chaddanta, the elephant's name, given in English as six-tusked.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fable about a noble animal.
what it means: forgiveness under the worst pressure; the wounded elephant helps the man who shot him.
what a scholar hears: Jataka 514 follows a grudge from one life into the next, and the elephant stops it; some readers stress that he honors the robe itself, whoever wears it.

839.title: The man-eating king
839.hook: a prince keeps his word to return to a captor, and changes him (Jataka 537)
839.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the Sutasoma story as an example of truthfulness (sacca), one of the ten perfections; keeping one's word is part of right speech in everyday practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chaddanta, the wounded elephant, cut his own tusks for the man who shot him. Your line was he helped the hunter. Did a small hurt come back, and did you answer it differently? Today, a prisoner who walks back to his captor. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

It starts with a promise to a stranger. A traveling brahmin arrives with verses to teach, and Prince Sutasoma tells him: wait here, I'll hear them when I come back from my bath. He never makes it back. On the road, a man who eats people snatches him and carries him off into the forest. Now the prince has a promise he can't keep and a captor who has no reason to let him go. Today, what he does about the promise.
screen: `A PROMISE TO A STRANGER.` → `SNATCHED ON THE ROAD.` → `A PROMISE HE CAN'T KEEP.`

segments.voice: First, the captor. In the Jataka he was once a king who acquired a taste for human flesh, was driven from his kingdom, and now lives in the forest as a man-eater. Second, the tears. Carried off, Sutasoma weeps, and the man-eater mocks him for fearing death. The prince says that's not why he's crying. He made a promise to a brahmin and left it unkept. Let me go, he says, and I'll keep it, and I'll come back. The man-eater lets him go, sure he'll never see him again. Third, the return. Sutasoma goes home, hears the verses, rewards the brahmin. His family begs him to stay. He goes back anyway, alone, to the man who plans to eat him. Fourth, the change. The man-eater is stunned. Who walks back to his own death to keep a word? He asks to hear the verses, and they're about the worth of keeping company with good people. He offers the prince a gift for each one. Among the gifts Sutasoma asks for: give up eating human flesh, and set your captives free. The man-eater agrees, and the captives go home. What's striking is that nothing here is forced. No army, no trick. The captor is changed by watching someone keep a promise that cost him everything. A kept word did what a sword couldn't. Tradition reads it as a picture of sacca, truthfulness, one of the ten perfections.
screen: `A KING TURNED MAN-EATER.` · `HE WEEPS FOR A PROMISE.` · `HE WALKS BACK ALONE.` · `HE ASKS: STOP.` · then, large: `HE CAME BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a promise. Let the breath settle. Then bring to mind something you said you'd do that's still open. A call you said you'd make. A form, a favor, a visit, a 'let me get back to you.' Small is fine. Picture actually doing it today: where you'll be, what you'll say. Notice any reluctance, the reasons it can wait. You don't have to fight them. Just let them be there while you hold the picture of the promise kept. The bell holds the time.
Sacca. Truth, truthfulness: the perfection behind the man-eating king who let Prince Sutasoma go, never expecting him back, and was changed when he returned. Today's word.
Your line: he came back. Keep the one open promise you pictured, before the day ends, even if no one's checking. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

what it means: keeping your word when it costs everything, and what that does to the person watching.
what a scholar hears: Jataka 537 is read as a tale of truthfulness; tradition links the man-eater to Angulimala, the killer the Buddha later turned.

840.title: The devoted son
840.hook: Sama cares for his blind parents and is shot by a king's arrow (Jataka 540)
840.tomorrow: The king who saw heaven and hell
840.howItsDone: Care for parents is part of everyday Buddhist ethics, and the Sama story is told as a picture of a child's devotion; some families make offerings in the names of parents, living and dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Prince Sutasoma walked back to a man-eater to keep his word, his sacca. Your line was he came back. Did you close the promise you pictured? Today ends the week, with a son at a river. Day eight hundred forty.

Early in the day, a young man kneels at a river to fill a water jar, and deer come down to drink beside him. They aren't afraid of him. In the Jataka his name is Sama, and the water isn't for him. Back at the hut are his mother and father, both blind, who depend on him for everything. Somewhere in the trees, a king out hunting has already raised his bow. Today, the arrow, and what Sama says when it hits.
screen: `A JAR AT THE RIVER.` → `DEER DRINK BESIDE HIM.` → `A KING RAISES HIS BOW.`

segments.voice: First, the household. Sama's parents lived as forest ascetics, and the story says they lost their sight to a snake's venom. From then on, Sama was their eyes and hands: water, fruit, washing, a path kept clear. Second, the arrow. The king, Piliyakkha, sees a figure among the deer and shoots to bring him down, so he can ask who he is before he runs. The poison takes hold. Sama falls, and the first thing he asks isn't for revenge. He asks who shot him and why, without anger. Then his thoughts turn to his parents. Who will bring them water now? Third, the king's turn. The question undoes him. He goes to the hut himself, tells the blind parents what he's done, and offers to serve them as their son did. Fourth, truth again. His parents and a goddess who watched over him speak acts of truth, true words about Sama's goodness, and the poison leaves him. He rises and teaches the king. Look back over the last few days and the same shape keeps returning. Sivi's eyes, the elephant's tusks, the prince who came back, and now Sama at the river. Each time, someone with every reason to think of himself thinks first of someone else, and pays a price for it. Tradition pairs Sama with the perfection of kindness, metta.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who raised you. Sit still for a moment. Bring to mind a parent, or whoever cared for you when you were small: living or gone, easy to love or not. If that's hard today, choose anyone older who once looked after you. Picture one ordinary thing they did for you, something they never mentioned. Rest with it. Then ask what they might need now: a call, a visit, a chore, or, if they've died, a moment of remembering them well. The bell holds the time.
Sama. The devoted son who cared for his blind parents and, shot by a king, thought first of them. Today's word.
Your line: who will bring them water. Do the one thing you pictured for the person who raised you, today, however small. Day eight hundred forty.
